idiom_name: hand-rolled Dictionary scope chain (Scope class + parent link)
implementation_notes: The BCL ships the containers, not the pattern: a Scope class holding a Dictionary<string, Symbol> plus a parent reference (or a stack of open scopes) with Define using TryAdd for duplicate detection and Lookup walking outward is the whole structure, and what replaces the classic class hierarchy is C#'s generics plus nullable reference types, which let the parent chain terminate in a nullable link instead of a sentinel global scope. Keep the hand-written table for your own language or DSL, where the scoping policy (block versus function scope, hoisting, local functions, using-declarations) is yours to encode. When the language under analysis is C# itself, Roslyn already ships the resolved model: SemanticModel.LookupSymbols(position) returns the symbols visible at a source position and GetSymbolInfo binds a syntax node to its ISymbol - the second variant.
pitfalls: Dictionary is thread-safe only for concurrent reads of an unmodified instance: a resolver published to parallel analyses must be per-thread or replaced by an immutable dictionary after the pass.

Nullable parent chains need a deliberate root: if the global scope is null instead of an explicit scope object, global names are indistinguishable from unresolved names and diagnostics become misleading.
Mutating a collection while enumerating it throws InvalidOperationException: reporting duplicates by iterating _symbols while defining more symbols in the same scope is an easy trap.

variants.name: Roslyn SemanticModel symbol lookup
variants.implementation_notes: When the target language is C#, Roslyn answers the same question without you modelling scopes: SemanticModel.LookupSymbols(position) returns the named symbols visible at a source position (respecting accessibility and nested scopes), GetSymbolsInScope lists the symbols of a scope, and GetSymbolInfo/GetDeclaredSymbol map syntax nodes to ISymbol. What replaces the classic structure is the compiler's own binder and symbol tables, so shadowing, usings, partial types and declaration merging are handled by the language implementation itself. The trade-offs are a heavyweight dependency (Microsoft.CodeAnalysis), a Compilation that must be built and refreshed for every edit, and the fact that only C#/VB are resolved - custom languages still need the hand-rolled variant.
pitfalls: LookupSymbols is positional: the same node yields different results inside a lambda, an initializer or a nested block - cache per position, not per node.
A SemanticModel is tied to one Compilation and SyntaxTree; holding models across edits keeps old bound symbols alive and returns stale answers, so build a new compilation per edit.
